text: Hello, this is Grete. The Rosens have gone into the dark with Mama, and Annemarie is alone in the rocking chair, waiting. This chapter is short and very quiet. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 12, and finish one full paragraph of your essay. Today’s question: what does it feel like to wait, not knowing?

Today’s reading move is about saying maybe. When you think something is a symbol, point to the exact words first. Then say what it might stand for, and why. A careful reader doesn’t say, this means. A careful reader says, this might mean, because. And then tries a second idea.

The model is a short sentence about not knowing where someone is. The sentence to fix is two sentences pushed together. Give the first one an ending, and the second one a capital to start. And look for one pair of words pressed into one, still waiting for its little mark.

This is review, so some of what you see is already right. In grammar and spelling, only tap what needs an editor. Read each line twice before you decide. Some of the hardest mistakes are the ones that look almost right.

Out of the woods now, and across the meadow. This is the last stretch of path. Four more go-words, and one of them describes a long line of people walking slowly together. When the last word is in place, look down at the harbor. Someone is waiting there.

Last match of the week. Try it with no misses at all. Then try something harder: use symbol and one other word together in a sentence about something in Chapters 9 to 12 that stands for more than itself.

This is a full editing pass. Some of these sentences are fine. Some have a little raised mark where it doesn’t belong, or no mark where one should be. Read each sentence slowly, the long way and the short way, and trust your ear.

Six words split into beats, and only some are split correctly. Clap each one out loud. If a split gives you a beat you didn’t clap, it needs fixing. Tap only those. Then fix one, and explain what went wrong.

Today’s Courage Watch is about waiting. During the war, my mother once sat up all night, waiting for my father to come home from a meeting he wouldn’t tell us about. She mended the same sock over and over. Waiting is a kind of courage nobody sees. Watch Annemarie alone in the rocking chair, and notice how she tries to stay calm.

This chapter is short, so read it slowly. Notice the clock in the hall, and the times Annemarie keeps track of. Notice the light outside the window. Then read the last page twice. After all that waiting, it moves very fast.

Now you write. The questions ask what wakes Annemarie, why Mama’s absence frightens her, and how her feelings about not knowing have changed since Chapter 9. Then you’ll build one full body paragraph, using every move from this week.

The third question asks you to look back across the whole week. In Chapter 9, Uncle Henrik said not knowing can help you be brave. Now Annemarie doesn’t know where her mother is. Does not knowing still feel like a help? Your answer can change. That’s exactly the point.

Today all the moves come together: a reason, a quote, a zoom on one word, a stretched so-what, and a knot back to your claim. Don’t try to make it perfect. Make it complete. This is the paragraph you’ll polish and publish next.

My grandmother had a tall clock like this in her hall. It struck every half hour, and at night you could hear it all through the house. On the worst nights of the war, I lay awake and counted the strikes. Every one meant someone still wasn’t home. Annemarie hears a clock like that in this chapter.

This card belongs to two fishermen, Børge Laursen and Jacob Andersen. In October 1943, they took their little boat, Marie, across the water to Sweden about ten times, each time with Jewish families hidden on board. Then they came back, and did it again. Uncle Henrik is made up. These two men are real.
Procession. A line of people moving forward together.
Intercede. To step in between, to help someone.
Concession. Something you give up to someone else.
Succeed. To do what you set out to do. And the path reaches the harbor.
